question_text: Minimum de-Broglie wavelength of photoelectrons emitted from a metal surface whose work function is $\phi$ and frequency of light incident on it is $\nu$ (given '$m$' is mass of electron and '$h$' is Planck's constant and $h\nu > \phi$) is
solution: The maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons is given by Einstein's photoelectric equation: $K_{\text{max}} = h\nu - \phi$. The minimum de-Broglie wavelength corresponds to maximum kinetic energy: $\lambda_{\text{min}} = \frac{h}{p_{\text{max}}} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mK_{\text{max}}}} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2m(h\nu - \phi)}}$.

question_text: What is the de-Broglie wavelength of an $\alpha$-particle accelerated through a potential difference '$V$'?
solution: For an $\alpha$-particle, charge $q = 2e$ and mass $m = 4m_p \approx 4 \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$. The de-Broglie wavelength is $\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}} = \frac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{\sqrt{2 \times (4 \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27}) \times (2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19})V}} \approx \frac{0.101}{\sqrt{V}}\text{ \AA}$.

question_text: The kinetic energy of an electron with de-Broglie wavelength of $0.3\text{ nm}$ is
solution: For an electron, $\lambda = \frac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}}\text{ nm} = \sqrt{\frac{150}{V}}\text{ \AA}$. Here $\lambda = 0.3\text{ nm} = 3\text{ \AA}$. Thus, $V = \frac{150}{\lambda^2} = \frac{150}{3^2} = \frac{150}{9} \approx 16.67\text{ V} \approx 16.8\text{ V}$. Therefore, the kinetic energy is $K = eV = 16.8\text{ eV}$.
The Compton effect involves an elastic collision between a photon and a stationary electron, which directly proves the particle nature of light (radiation).

question_text: In de-Broglie hypothesis, the momentum is inversely proportional to
solution: According to the de-Broglie hypothesis, $p = \frac{h}{\lambda} \implies p \propto \frac{1}{\lambda}$. Also, since $p = mv$, $p \propto v$, which means $p \propto \frac{1}{(1/v)}$ (i.e. inversely proportional to $1/v$). Hence, momentum is inversely proportional to both $\lambda$ and $\frac{1}{v}$.
